summary: Describes an RTP payload format for the Essential Video Coding (EVC) standard, ISO/IEC 23094-1, developed by MPEG. It lets one or more NAL units go in a packet and splits larger ones across packets, for uses like videoconferencing and Internet video streaming.

eli5.summary: Video must be cut into small pieces to travel over the internet. This explains how to pack and number pieces of EVC video so they can be put back together.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for evc
what is an evc aggregation packet
how are evc nal units fragmented in rtp
subtitle: How to chop Essential Video Coding (EVC) video into RTP packets and put it back together at the receiver.

tldr.problem: EVC (ISO/IEC 23094-1) produces video as NAL units of very different sizes, and these need to travel over RTP in packets that fit the network and can be reassembled in the right order.
tldr.mechanism: Three payload structures are defined: a single NAL unit packet, an aggregation packet that bundles small NAL units from one access unit, and fragmentation units that split one large NAL unit across packets. Media type parameters and SDP rules describe and negotiate the stream.
tldr.outcome: EVC video can be carried over RTP in videoconferencing, streaming and similar uses, with a design deliberately close to the earlier H.264, HEVC and VVC payload formats.

today: RFC 9584 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2024 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the RTP payload format for EVC and builds on RFC 3550.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Lineage
sections.content:
The Essential Video Coding standard, ISO/IEC 23094-1, was published in 2020. One goal of MPEG was to keep EVC's Baseline profile essentially royalty-free, while more advanced profiles follow reasonable and non-discriminatory licensing terms. Both are reported to give coding efficiency gains over HEVC and AVC under certain configurations.

This document defines an RTP payload format for EVC. It shares its basic design with the NAL unit based payload formats for H.264 (RFC 6184), SVC (RFC 6190), HEVC (RFC 7798) and VVC (RFC 9328). That was a conscious choice, since the H.264 format is described as widely deployed and well known to implementers. Some mechanisms from RFC 6190 were reused because EVC supports temporal scalability, but no higher forms of scalability.

The payload format covers the use of the RTP header, three payload structures, carrying all NAL units of one bitstream in a single RTP stream, media type parameters for SDP, and RTCP feedback messages.
sections.eli5: People already know how to send other kinds of video over the internet. This new recipe copies the old ones so engineers do not have to learn everything again.

sections.title: EVC and Its NAL Unit Header
sections.content:
Like AVC, HEVC and VVC, EVC has a Video Coding Layer for the coding tools and a Network Abstraction Layer (NAL) for the systems and transport side. Video travels as NAL units. EVC has a Baseline and a Main profile, plus still-image variants of each. It uses a sequence parameter set (SPS) and two picture-level sets, the PPS and the APS, and it supports up to six temporal layers, signalled in the NAL unit header.

The NAL unit header is two bytes: F (1 bit, the forbidden zero bit), Type (6 bits, holding the NAL unit type plus 1), TID (3 bits, the temporal identifier), Reserve (5 bits) and E (1 bit, the extension flag). The type field MUST NOT be zero. If the NAL unit type is 23 or less it is a VCL NAL unit, which carries coded picture data.

The RFC says implementers still have to read the ISO/IEC standard itself. This payload format only handles transport.
sections.eli5: Each piece of video wears a small name tag at the front saying what kind of piece it is and how important it is.

sections.title: RTP Header and Payload Header
sections.content:
The RTP header follows RFC 3550. The marker bit is set on the last packet of an access unit. The timestamp uses a 90 kHz clock, which MUST be used, and receivers MUST use the RTP timestamp for display even when the bitstream has picture timing SEI messages. NAL units with no timing of their own, such as parameter sets, take the timestamp of their access unit. A single SSRC is used for all parts of one bitstream. The payload type is assigned outside this document.

The first two bytes of every RTP payload are the payload header, with the same fields as the NAL unit header, whatever the payload structure. A lower TID means higher importance, so more important NAL units MAY be better protected against loss.
sections.eli5: Every packet starts with the same little label, so the receiver always knows what is inside and how much it matters.

sections.title: The Three Payload Structures
sections.content:
A receiver tells the structure apart by the Type field of the payload header.

A single NAL unit packet holds exactly one NAL unit. Its own NAL unit header doubles as the payload header, optionally followed by a 16-bit DONL field, then the NAL unit payload.

An aggregation packet (AP) has Type=56 and carries two or more aggregation units from one access unit, in decoding order. Each unit has a 16-bit size field followed by the NAL unit. An AP MUST NOT mix access units, MUST NOT be nested and MUST NOT contain FUs. Its F bit is 0 only if every aggregated NAL unit has F equal to 0, and its TID is the smallest TID of the aggregated units. Its size SHOULD keep the IP packet below the path MTU.

A fragmentation unit (FU) has Type=57 and carries part of one NAL unit. An FU header of one byte holds an S bit (start), an E bit (end) and a 6-bit FuType copied from the fragmented NAL unit. Fragments MUST be sent in consecutive order with ascending sequence numbers, and S and E MUST NOT both be 1. If an FU is lost, the receiver SHOULD discard the following FUs of the same NAL unit, unless its decoder copes with incomplete NAL units. APs MUST NOT be fragmented and FUs MUST NOT be nested.
sections.eli5: A small note can share an envelope with other small notes. A big note is cut up and sent in several envelopes marked first, middle and last.

sections.title: Packetization, Decoding Order and De-packetization
sections.content:
If sprop-max-don-diff is 0, NAL units MUST be sent in decoding order. If it is greater than 0, transmission order MAY differ, and each packet then carries a DONL field (the low 16 bits of the decoding order number). The receiver derives an absolute order, AbsDon, from these values, with wraparound handled around 32768 and 65536. The aggregation unit that follows another in an AP gets the previous DON plus 1 modulo 65536.

Senders SHOULD aggregate small NAL units, such as parameter sets and SEI, ideally with the VCL NAL unit they belong to when the MTU allows. A single NAL unit packet MUST be used for carrying precisely one NAL unit.

The receiver removes duplicate and outdated packets, then extracts NAL units: it takes the payload of a single NAL unit packet, splits an AP, or concatenates FU payloads from the S packet to the E packet and rebuilds the NAL unit header. Types 0 to 55 may go to the decoder; types 56 to 62 MUST NOT. With sprop-max-don-diff equal to 0 the de-packetization buffer is zero bytes. Otherwise the receiver buffers until the spread of AbsDon values reaches that parameter, then releases NAL units in increasing AbsDon order.

For feedback, a PLI SHOULD lead an EVC sender to send an IDR picture and the relevant parameter sets. A FIR MUST lead to an IDR picture, with parameter sets unless they are known to be established. Senders MUST NOT send SLI or RPSI messages.
sections.eli5: If pieces arrive jumbled, each one carries a counter so the receiver can sort them into the right order. Small pieces are bundled to save envelopes.

sections.title: Media Type Parameters
sections.content:
The media type is video/evc, defined only for transfer over RTP, and it has been registered with IANA. Receivers MUST ignore any parameter not specified in this document. Parameters starting with sprop describe the stream the sender will send, and the sender, not the receiver, chooses them.

  • profile-id, level-id, toolset-id: profile, level and tool constraints. When profile-id is absent, 0 (Baseline) MUST be inferred. When level-id is absent, 90 (level 3) MUST be inferred.
  • max-recv-level-id: the highest level a receiver supports, from 0 to 255.
  • sprop-sps, sprop-pps, sprop-sei: comma-separated base64 NAL units sent out of band.
  • sprop-max-don-diff: 0 to 32767, default 0.
  • sprop-depack-buf-bytes: required buffer size, 0 to 4294967295. It MUST be present and greater than 0 when sprop-max-don-diff is greater than 0.
  • depack-buf-cap: the receiver's buffer capacity in bytes, 1 to 4294967295.
sections.eli5: These are the settings you tell the other side about before the video starts, like which quality level you can handle and how big a sorting tray you have.

sections.title: Using SDP and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
In SDP, the media name is video, the encoding name is evc and the clock rate MUST be 90000. Most parameters go in the a=fmtp line.

In an offer/answer exchange under RFC 3264, the answerer either keeps every configuration parameter as offered or removes the payload type. The one exception is that level-id may be lowered, but not raised above the offer. Unlike usual, sprop-max-don-diff and sprop-depack-buf-bytes describe the stream the declaring party will send, not what it can receive. An interleaved offer, with sprop-max-don-diff above zero, MUST include sprop-depack-buf-bytes.

For multicast, the configuration, including level-id, MUST be used symmetrically, so level-id cannot change. In declarative uses such as RTSP or SAP, parameters describe only the actual bitstream, and a receiver that cannot support them MUST reject or not join the session. Parameter sets sent out of band MAY also be sent in-band, and later in-band ones may update them.
sections.eli5: Two sides agree on a video quality they both can handle. If one cannot manage the high level, it can say 'lower, please', but it cannot ask for more.

sections.title: Security and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Apart from one feature, the RFC knows of no security threats beyond those common to RTP payload formats, and it leaves confidentiality, integrity and source authentication to the RTP security options in use. Applications SHOULD use strong security mechanisms. Because compression is end to end, encryption needs to be done after compression.

EVC is called particularly vulnerable to denial of service by injected pathological data, since it is simple to craft NAL units that affect the decoding of many later ones. Data origin authentication and integrity protection of at least the RTP packet are therefore RECOMMENDED. The user data SEI message can carry arbitrary bitstrings, even active content like JavaScript, so decoders cannot naively trust it. The safest handling is to discard it.

End-to-end protection stops a MANE from doing media-aware work other than dropping whole packets, unless it is a trusted part of the security context.

Congestion control follows RTP and its profile. Best-effort users MUST monitor packet loss. The key tool in EVC is temporal scalability: a sender can drop NAL units from higher temporal sub-layers, those with a large TID, until the bitrate is acceptable.
sections.eli5: Someone could sneak in a very hard puzzle to tire the receiver out, so it is wise to check who sent the packets. If the road gets crowded, the sender can drop the less important frames.

fields.name: F
fields.desc: Forbidden zero bit; required to be zero in EVC.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: NAL unit type plus 1; must not be zero.

fields.name: TID
fields.desc: Temporal identifier of the NAL unit.

fields.name: Reserve
fields.desc: Equal to the EVC version; reserved for future use.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: Extension flag; 1 is reserved for future use.

cells: Two or more NAL units of one access unit
A part of one NAL unit

fields.name: S
fields.desc: 1 on the first fragment of a NAL unit.

fields.name: E
fields.desc: 1 on the last fragment of a NAL unit.

fields.name: FuType
fields.desc: Same as the Type of the fragmented NAL unit.

viz.caption: OFFER AND ANSWER EXAMPLE FROM THE RFC

data.title: Offer, then answer at a lower level
data.code:
Offerer->Answerer:
  m=video 49170 RTP/AVP 98
  a=rtpmap:98 evc/90000
  a=fmtp:98 profile-id=1; level_id=90;

Answerer->Offerer:
  m=video 49170 RTP/AVP 98
  a=rtpmap:98 evc/90000
  a=fmtp:98 profile-id=1; level_id=60
